review_note: Keep short impact slides and deliberate teaching repetition. Align scope and reader-address changes with the lecture; simplify speaker notes that explain the course's virtue.

edits.before: - Pause here. Let the room notice that everyone already knows this, and nobody was told.
edits.after: - Pause here before showing a possible reply.
edits.reason: Preserve the pause without assuming every student already knows the convention.

edits.before: - Read it twice. It is the whole argument and it is on every page of the site.
edits.after: - Read it twice, pausing between the two clauses.
edits.reason: Keep the delivery instruction and remove the promotional explanation.

edits.before: - The run sheet promise matters to a lot of people in this room. Make it explicitly.
edits.after: - Say that the lab run sheets are available in advance.
edits.reason: Replace a prediction about the room with the information students need.

edits.before:
- This is the engineering scandal the course is named for.
- Researchers have been writing the rules down for over fifty years, for other researchers, in a register nobody outside the field reads.
edits.after: - Researchers have been writing the rules down for over fifty years, for other researchers.
edits.reason: The slide already carries the joke; the notes need only the supporting context.

edits.before: - We read the abstract, not the paper. Do not list the six; say so out loud, because the room should see the course obeying its own citation rule.
edits.after: - We read the abstract, not the paper. Say so; do not list the six.
edits.reason: Retain honest attribution without directing the teacher to perform the course's integrity.

edits.before: - The finding that survives is the one that matters here.
edits.reason: The slide states the finding; this note adds only emphasis.

edits.before:
The course's position is not "don't take it".

It is that you should be able to **see the fork while you're standing at it**.
edits.after:
**See the fork while you're standing at it.**

Then decide whether this is the conversation you want to start.
edits.reason: Keep the fork image and agency while removing institutional self-commentary.

edits.before: Everything so far assumes the opening **obliges** you. The course hasn't earned that yet.
edits.after: Why does an opening make a reply **expected**?
edits.reason: Align with the lecture's direct question.

edits.before: - This is the honest gap, and the room should watch you close it rather than paper over it.
edits.after: - Name the evidence gap before introducing Stivers and Rossano.
edits.reason: Turn a claim about honesty into a concrete teaching instruction.

edits.before: **If replies are hard for you:** you may have been treating every opening as maximum obligation. Many are turned down low. A nod answers a nod. You can match the level you were given.
edits.after: **If replies are hard for you:** you can match the level you were given. A nod can answer a nod; a person already walking away may not be inviting a conversation.
edits.reason: Carry through the lecture's removal of assumptions about the reader.

edits.before: - Collect the changes on the board: position, wording, timing, body. That list is the week's real artefact, and week 4 measures it in milliseconds.
edits.after: - Collect the changes on the board: position, wording, timing, body. Keep the list for week 4's work on timing.
edits.reason: Keep the board work and cross-reference; cut the repeated declaration of significance.

edits.before: If you run the handshake without effort, the spec read as the obvious. That's because you've run it ten thousand times, not because it's simple.
edits.after: If you run the handshake without effort, familiarity can make its rules hard to see.
edits.reason: Remove the invented count and align the slide with the lecture.
